items.title: New ISO standard enables mobile robots from different vendors to work together
items.summary: A3 has published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communication and interoperability among industrial mobile robots. This standard establishes common communication requirements for mobile robots from different vendors operating in the same facility. It specifies how robots, fleet managers, and other equipment can exchange information such as location, status, and tasking. Adopting this standard is expected to reduce path interference, improve system efficiency, and foster market competition. Furthermore, the standard covers communication with external systems like ERP tools and building automation.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, "New ISO standard enables mobile robots from different vendors to work together". This report details the publication of a new international standard designed to establish common communication and interoperability among industrial mobile robots from various vendors operating within the same facility. The standard specifies the requirements for how robots, fleet managers, and associated equipment can exchange critical data including location, operational status, and tasking information. This framework is intended to minimize path interference, enhance overall system efficiency, and promote market competition in the sector. The standard also addresses communication protocols for interfacing with external systems such as enterprise resource planning tools and building automation systems. Adoption of this standard is expected to create a more cohesive operational environment for industrial automation. The development signals a step toward standardized industrial robotics integration across diverse supply chains.

items.title: ROS Discourse General: Intrinsic Core released: Open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control, motion planning and more
items.summary: Intrinsic Core was released as an open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control framework for industrial robotics. It provides a hardware-agnostic runtime, SDK, and framework for real-time control, motion planning, and grasp planning. The release includes a pre-configured setup, including simulation tools and a reference solution called the Open Machine Tending Solution (OMTS). Community members are actively building variations on OMTS, demonstrating its practical application in tasks like picking up and inserting objects. Intrinsic Core aims to be practical and open by fostering community collaboration.
items.audio_script: From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Intrinsic Core released: Open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control, motion planning and more". This report details the release of Intrinsic Core, an open-source, ROS-compatible real-time control framework designed for industrial robotics. The framework provides a hardware-agnostic runtime, SDK, and framework encompassing real-time control, motion planning, and grasp planning capabilities. The release includes a pre-configured setup with simulation tools and a reference solution known as the Open Machine Tending Solution, or OMTS. Community members are currently developing variations of OMTS, applying the framework to practical tasks such as object picking and insertion. This development emphasizes a collaborative approach to practical industrial automation. The open nature of Intrinsic Core establishes a new foundation for robotics development and real-time system integration.

items.title: Welcome, DG-4F!
items.summary: Tesollo’s four-finger robotic hand scores 6/10 overall, with a Degree of Freedom rating of 4/5 and a Strength rating of 2/5. This scoring highlights a greater capability for dexterity compared to grip strength within the assessment framework. The assessment emphasizes that flexibility and strength must be evaluated separately based on specific handling requirements. The hand is listed as in production with an advertised price of USD 12,000 from Tesollo in South Korea. Buyers should evaluate specific dexterity and force requirements rather than relying solely on the overall score.

items.title: Nvidia humanoid platforms rely on robot hands with China ties
items.summary: Nvidia's humanoid reference platforms utilize mechanical hands from Chinese startup Wuji and hands from Singapore-based Sharpa. Both suppliers have significant ties to Shanghai, centralizing Chinese hardware development for Nvidia's robotics software research. These systems demonstrate that robot training packages rely on specialized suppliers for body and manipulation hardware rather than a single manufacturer. Practitioners note trade-offs between the hands concerning task performance, thermal behavior, and cost. Hand selection is thus framed as balancing these practical constraints in humanoid development.

items.title: Tutor Intelligence raises $75 million to scale robot workforce
items.summary: Tutor Intelligence raised $75 million in a Series B round, totaling $117 million, led by Andreessen Horowitz. This funding will support training their frontier robot foundation models and deploying their robot workers, Sonny and Cassie. The company bridges the gap between robot capabilities and human capabilities by using real-world deployment data for training. Tutor utilizes internet-connected robots operated by remote "tutors" to perform real work in production environments. This approach creates a self-reinforcing cycle that makes robots smarter, more affordable, and enables broader workforce automation.

items.title: Humanoid Robot Batteries Could Become an $850 Million Market by 2037, IDTechEx Forecasts
items.summary: The market for humanoid robot batteries is projected to reach US$850 million by 2037, according to IDTechEx. This forecast is based on a projected ten-year compound annual growth rate of 34.2%. The analysis considers spare batteries for swapping alongside demand from new robots. The report evaluates various battery technologies against performance metrics for industrial, commercial, and domestic humanoids. The demand is also influenced by solutions like battery swapping to extend operational time for robots.
items.audio_script: From Humanoids Daily, "Humanoid Robot Batteries Could Become an $850 Million Market by 2037, IDTechEx Forecasts". This report details the projected market size for batteries powering humanoid robots, forecasting a total market value of eight hundred fifty million US dollars by the year two thousand thirty-seven. The forecast is derived from an anticipated ten-year compound annual growth rate of thirty-four point two percent, factoring in both the demand for new robot batteries and the necessity for spare batteries in swapping systems. The analysis incorporated performance metrics across various battery technologies assessed for industrial, commercial, and domestic humanoid applications, with consideration given to solutions that extend robot operational time through battery swapping. This projection highlights the growing commercial viability of energy solutions within the humanoid robotics sector. Attention should be directed toward advancements in energy density and swapping technology moving forward.

items.title: Opinion: What happens when the robot is wrong?
items.summary: Increased robot speed necessitates a clear process for experienced operators to challenge machine decisions to prevent errors from spreading. Safety procedures must remain paramount, and challenges should not supersede physical safeguarding measures like emergency stops. Effective commissioning should include rehearsals involving false positives and conflicting instructions to test human response and decision-making authority. Systems must retain exception records detailing operator challenges, evidence, and responses across shifts. Ultimately, a successful system evaluation should include metrics for human-AI teaming and operator understanding alongside traditional performance measures.
items.audio_script: From Robotics & Automation News, "Opinion: What happens when the robot is wrong?". This story examines the necessary procedures for experienced operators to challenge machine decisions to prevent errors from propagating. Increased robot speed requires a clear process for human intervention to maintain safety. Effective commissioning protocols must incorporate rehearsals involving false positives and conflicting instructions to assess human response and decision-making authority. Systems must maintain exception records documenting operator challenges, evidence, and responses across shifts. Successful system evaluation requires metrics assessing human-AI teaming alongside traditional performance measures. This emphasizes the need for robust, documented human oversight in advanced automation systems.

items.title: Muscle coordination can be mimicked by electric motors – it could lead to improved robots
items.summary: Electric motors were used to build a physical model simulating muscle coordination. The model demonstrated that muscle-like behavior emerges from the physical arrangement of motors and their shared mechanical structure, not from continuous programming. This setup showed that motors can coordinate by briefly engaging a shared backbone, allowing forces to be transmitted collectively. This principle of coordination without a central conductor could lead to simpler and more adaptable designs for robots. These findings suggest a path toward creating more organic and adaptive robotic systems.
items.audio_script: From Robohub, "Muscle coordination can be mimicked by electric motors – it could lead to improved robots". This story details research demonstrating that muscle-like coordination can be mimicked using electric motors, showing that muscle behavior emerges from the physical arrangement of motors and their shared mechanical structure rather than continuous programming. Researchers constructed a physical model utilizing electric motors to simulate muscle coordination, revealing that motor-like behavior arises from the physical arrangement and shared mechanical structure of the motors, not from direct programming commands. The setup demonstrated that motors can coordinate by briefly engaging a shared backbone, permitting the collective transmission of forces, establishing a principle of coordination without a central conductor. This method suggests a pathway toward developing simpler and more adaptable designs for robotic systems. This research indicates a direction toward creating more organic and adaptive robotic systems.

items.title: Churchill Capital XI shareholders approve $2.5B Agility Robotics humanoid SPAC
items.summary: Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the $2.5 billion SPAC business combination with Agility Robotics. This move allows Agility to become a publicly-traded company, with the transaction expected to close on November 4th. The funding will support commercial expansion, customer deployments, and manufacturing capacity for the Digit humanoid robot business. Agility already has customer deployments with GXO Logistics and is expanding into manufacturing. The company is pursuing commercial markets in logistics and manufacturing with a product roadmap for Digit 5.

This action authorizes Agility Robotics to become a publicly traded company with the transaction anticipated to finalize on November fourth. The funding secured is designated to support the commercial expansion of the Digit humanoid robot business, encompassing customer deployments, and the necessary manufacturing capacity. Agility Robotics currently has existing customer deployments with GXO Logistics and is advancing manufacturing operations alongside its product roadmap for Digit five targeting commercial markets in logistics and manufacturing. This development signals further investment and tangible progression in the commercialization of humanoid robotics technology.

The announcement was first published on the Robotics Institute Carnegie Mellon University website.

items.title: Welcome, YMBot D!
items.summary: YMBot D is a foldable, wheeled humanoid robot developed by Jiangsu Yunmu Intelligent Manufacturing Technology Co., Ltd. It measures 165 cm tall and weighs 100 kg, featuring 22 degrees of freedom and two articulated arms. The robot is designed for tasks like obstacle avoidance, sorting goods, and product assembly using its mobile base and dexterous hands. It is listed as in production with a price of USD 35,000 and utilizes an Intel 12th generation CPU. The robot represents a direction in humanoid development combining mobility with object handling for industrial applications.

items.title: Welcome, Max!
items.summary: Max is Meta's first humanoid robot prototype, developed with Fourier for home assistance research. Standing 150 cm and weighing 48 kg, it features humanoid form, five-fingered hands, and a face screen. Documented capabilities include obstacle avoidance, stair walking, and operating a dishwasher, linking movement with household object manipulation. Its skill score is low (3/10), placing it in the developing category for general-purpose robots. The prototype serves as a platform for researching physical systems for home assistance.

items.title: Welcome, YMBot H!
items.summary: YMBot H is a wheeled, humanoid service robot developed by Jiangsu Yunmu Intelligent Manufacturing Technology Co., Ltd. It is designed for visitor engagement in public spaces, featuring a humanlike appearance, dual arms, and a mobile base. Ultimately, YMBot H is positioned as a preliminary service platform emphasizing mobile humanoid form over advanced physical task performance.

items.title: Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos
items.summary: NVIDIA Cosmos provides world foundation models and tools to address sensor adaptation and reliable deployment challenges in physical AI. The Cosmos Framework offers modular tools for training, optimization, and inference across various models. Simulation recipes allow for generating synchronized video and LiDAR data for applications like autonomous vehicles and robotics. Cosmos NIM microservices accelerate inference through techniques like quantization and speculative decoding on GPUs. Developers can use the framework to train models, perform reinforcement learning, and deploy optimized models using specialized skills.

Simulation recipes enable the generation of synchronized video and LiDAR data for applications such as autonomous vehicles and robotics.
